def rank_cov(x: Sequence[F], y: Sequence[F]) -> F:
    """Rank covariance S_xy = sum (r_x - mean)(r_y - mean)."""
    rx, ry = midranks(x), midranks(y)
    mx, my = sum(rx) / len(rx), sum(ry) / len(ry)
    return sum((a - mx) * (b - my) for a, b in zip(rx, ry))


def spearman(x: Sequence[F], y: Sequence[F]) -> float:
    """Spearman's rho = S_xy / sqrt(S_xx S_yy)  (float; exact parts printed)."""
    return float(rank_cov(x, y)) / sqrt(float(rank_cov(x, x)) * float(rank_cov(y, y)))


def part_one_audit() -> None:
    rule("1. The measured table and the three Spearman coefficients (exact)")
    header = f"{'domain':<10}{'entropy':>10}{'top-8':>10}{'head agr':>11}{'k*@512':>9}"
    print(header)
    print("-" * len(header))
    for i, d in enumerate(DOMAINS):
        k = ">24" if d == "prose-fr" else str(int(KSTAR[i]))
        print(f"{d:<10}{float(ENTROPY[i]):>10.3f}{float(TOP8[i]):>10.3f}"
              f"{float(HEAD_AGR[i]):>11.3f}{k:>9}")

    print("\nMidranks")
    for name, col in (("entropy", ENTROPY), ("top-8", TOP8),
                      ("head agr", HEAD_AGR), ("k*", KSTAR)):
        print(f"  {name:<9}: {[frac(r) for r in midranks(col)]}")

    s_kk = rank_cov(KSTAR, KSTAR)
    print(f"\nS_(k*,k*) = {frac(s_kk)}   S_(ent,ent) = {frac(rank_cov(ENTROPY, ENTROPY))}"
          f"   S_(top8,top8) = {frac(rank_cov(TOP8, TOP8))}"
          f"   S_(head,head) = {frac(rank_cov(HEAD_AGR, HEAD_AGR))}")

    print("\nRank covariances with k* and the resulting rho:")
    reported = {"entropy": -0.60, "top-8 mass": +0.80, "head agreement": -0.40}
    for name, col, exact in (
        ("entropy", ENTROPY, "7/(2*sqrt(95))"),
        ("top-8 mass", TOP8, "-11/38"),
        ("head agreement", HEAD_AGR, "-8/sqrt(95)"),
    ):
        print(f"  {name:<15} S = {frac(rank_cov(col, KSTAR)):>6}"
              f"   rho = {spearman(col, KSTAR):+.4f}  (= {exact})"
              f"   reported: {reported[name]:+.2f}")

    order = sorted((("entropy", abs(spearman(ENTROPY, KSTAR))),
                    ("top-8 mass", abs(spearman(TOP8, KSTAR))),
                    ("head agreement", abs(spearman(HEAD_AGR, KSTAR)))),
                   key=lambda p: -p[1])
    print("\n  |rho| ranking (recomputed): " +
          " > ".join(f"{n} ({v:.3f})" for n, v in order))
    print("  reported ranking:            top-8 mass > entropy > head agreement")
    print("  => the ranking of the three predictors is exactly inverted.")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Robustness: censoring and tie-breaks
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------


def part_two_robustness() -> None:
    rule("2. Robustness of the audit")
    print("(a) prose-fr's knee is censored at '>24'.  Every reading v > 20 gives")
    print("    the same midranks, hence the same coefficients:")
    for v in (F(21), F(24), F(25), F(64), F(1000)):
        col = [F(12), F(16), F(16), F(20), v]
        print(f"    v = {frac(v):>6}:  S_top8 = {frac(rank_cov(TOP8, col)):>6},"
              f"  S_entropy = {frac(rank_cov(ENTROPY, col)):>4},"
              f"  S_headAgr = {frac(rank_cov(HEAD_AGR, col)):>4}")

    print("\n(b) Ordinal tie-breaks.  The two ties are top-8 (code = prose-en) and")
    print("    k* (prose-en = math).  Enumerate all admissible integer rankings:")

    def ordinal_rankings(col: Sequence[F]) -> Iterable[Tuple[int, ...]]:
        """All bijections onto {1..5} that are strictly monotone in the data."""
        n = len(col)
        for perm in permutations(range(1, n + 1)):
            ok = all((col[i] < col[j]) <= (perm[i] < perm[j]) and
                     (perm[i] < perm[j]) <= (col[i] <= col[j])
                     for i in range(n) for j in range(n) if i != j)
            if ok:
                yield perm

    def zcov(r: Sequence[int], s: Sequence[int]) -> int:
        return sum((a - 3) * (b - 3) for a, b in zip(r, s))

    ks = list(ordinal_rankings(KSTAR))
    for name, col in (("entropy", ENTROPY), ("top-8", TOP8), ("head agr", HEAD_AGR)):
        vals = sorted({zcov(r, s) for r in ordinal_rankings(col) for s in ks})
        rhos = sorted(float(F(v, 10)) for v in vals)  # rho = S / 10 for two full rankings
        print(f"    {name:<9}: rank covariances over all tie-breaks = {vals}"
              f"  -> rho in {rhos}")
    print("\n    top-8/knee is negative under EVERY tie-break (rho <= -0.1);")
    print("    entropy/knee is positive under every tie-break (rho >= +0.2);")
    print("    head-agreement/knee is <= -0.7 under every tie-break.")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Exact permutation calculus on five items
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------


def dsq(perm: Sequence[int]) -> int:
    """Squared rank displacement sum (sigma(i) - i)^2 for a permutation of 0..4."""
    return sum((perm[i] - i) ** 2 for i in range(len(perm)))


def rho_from_D(D: int) -> F:
    """Spearman's rho at n = 5:  rho = 1 - 6D/(n(n^2-1)) = 1 - D/20."""
    return F(1) - F(D, 20)


def part_three_power() -> None:
    rule("3. Exact permutation calculus at n = 5")
    all_perms = list(permutations(range(5)))
    assert len(all_perms) == 120
    dist: Dict[int, int] = {}
    for p in all_perms:
        dist[dsq(p)] = dist.get(dsq(p), 0) + 1
    print("Null distribution of D = sum (sigma(i)-i)^2 over S_5 (120 permutations):")
    print(f"  {'D':>4} {'rho':>9} {'count':>6}")
    for D in sorted(dist):
        print(f"  {D:>4} {float(rho_from_D(D)):>9.2f} {dist[D]:>6}")

    bar = sum(c for D, c in dist.items() if abs(rho_from_D(D)) >= F(7, 10))
    print(f"\n  #{{ |rho| >= 0.7 }} = {bar} of 120  ->  exact size "
          f"{frac(F(bar, 120))} = {float(F(bar,120)):.4f}")
    print("  A pre-registered |rho| >= 0.7 bar is therefore roughly a 23% test,")
    print("  not a 5% test: nearly one random pairing in four clears it.")

    tail34 = sum(c for D, c in dist.items() if D >= 34)
    tail38 = sum(c for D, c in dist.items() if D >= 38)
    print(f"\n  one-sided tails:  #{{D >= 34}} = {tail34} -> p = {frac(F(tail34,120))}"
          f" = {float(F(tail34,120)):.4f}")
    print(f"                    #{{D >= 38}} = {tail38} -> p = {frac(F(tail38,120))}"
          f" = {float(F(tail38,120)):.4f}")

    print("\n  Head agreement vs. the knee, the strongest column in the table:")
    r = (4, 3, 5, 2, 1)
    for label, s in (("tie -> prose-en first", (1, 2, 3, 4, 5)),
                     ("tie -> math first    ", (1, 3, 2, 4, 5))):
        D = sum((a - b) ** 2 for a, b in zip(r, s))
        p = F(sum(c for Dp, c in dist.items() if Dp >= D), 120)
        verdict = "significant at 5%" if p < F(1, 20) else "NOT significant at 5%"
        print(f"    {label}:  D = {D:>3}, rho = {float(rho_from_D(D)):+.2f},"
              f"  p = {frac(p)} = {float(p):.4f}  ({verdict})")
    print("\n  The tie in the data, not the data, decides the verdict.")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Capture curves, knees, and the exact tail reduction
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------

CaptureCurve = Callable[[int], F]


def knee_at(cum: CaptureCurve, tau: F, bound: int = 100000) -> int:
    """Least k with cum(k) >= tau."""
    for k in range(bound + 1):
        if cum(k) >= tau:
            return k
    raise ValueError("knee not reached within bound")


def tail_knee(cum: CaptureCurve, r: int, tau: F, bound: int = 100000) -> int:
    """Least j with cum(r + j) >= tau: the knee computed inside the residual."""
    for j in range(bound + 1):
        if cum(r + j) >= tau:
            return j
    raise ValueError("tail knee not reached within bound")


def residual(cum: CaptureCurve, r: int) -> F:
    return F(1) - cum(r)


def uniform_profile(tau: F, k: int) -> CaptureCurve:
    """Capture curve rising linearly to tau at key k: cum(n) = min(1, n*tau/k)."""
    return lambda n: min(F(1), F(n) * tau / k)


def staged_profile(c: F, tau: F, r: int, k: int) -> CaptureCurve:
    """Head mass c at key r, then a linear ramp reaching tau exactly at key k."""
    step = (tau - c) / (F(k) - F(r))

    def cum(j: int) -> F:
        if j == 0:
            return F(0)
        return min(F(1), c + F(max(j - r, 0)) * step)

    return cum


def part_four_tail_reduction() -> None:
    rule("4. The exact tail reduction  k* = r + (knee of the residual curve)")
    tau = F(9, 10)
    P = staged_profile(F(1, 2), tau, 8, 20)
    r = 8
    print(f"  tolerance tau = {frac(tau)}, head budget r = {r}")
    print(f"  cum(r) = {frac(P(r))} < tau, residual = {frac(residual(P, r))}")
    print(f"  k*        = {knee_at(P, tau)}")
    print(f"  r + tailKnee = {r} + {tail_knee(P, r, tau)} = {r + tail_knee(P, r, tau)}")
    print("  -> the knee splits exactly into head budget + tail knee.")

    print("\n  Two curves that agree from key r on have the same knee, whatever")
    print("  their heads do:")
    Q = staged_profile(F(1, 2), tau, 8, 20)

    def Q_bumped(j: int) -> F:  # same values from r on, different head
        return F(0) if j == 0 else (min(F(4, 10), F(j) * F(1, 10)) if j < r else Q(j))

    print(f"    head values differ:  P(3) = {frac(P(3))} vs Q'(3) = {frac(Q_bumped(3))}")
    print(f"    knees agree:         k*(P) = {knee_at(P, tau)},"
          f"  k*(Q') = {knee_at(Q_bumped, tau)}")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Head/knee decoupling
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------


def part_five_decoupling() -> None:
    rule("5. Head mass determines nothing about the knee")
    tau = F(9, 10)
    print(f"  tolerance tau = {frac(tau)};  head statistic = top-8 mass cum(8)\n")
    print("  (a) Same head mass, any knee you like:")
    for k in (9, 12, 25, 200):
        P = staged_profile(F(1, 2), tau, 8, k)
        print(f"      cum(8) = {frac(P(8))},  k* = {knee_at(P, tau):>4}  (target {k})")
    print("      => no function g with k* = g(top-8 mass) can exist.")

    print("\n  (b) Both signs of the head-mass/knee association are realisable:")
    P = staged_profile(F(1, 2), tau, 8, 9)
    Q = staged_profile(F(3, 4), tau, 8, 12)
    print(f"      more head mass, later knee:  {frac(P(8))} -> k* = {knee_at(P, tau)}"
          f" ;  {frac(Q(8))} -> k* = {knee_at(Q, tau)}")
    P2 = staged_profile(F(1, 2), tau, 8, 12)
    Q2 = staged_profile(F(3, 4), tau, 8, 9)
    print(f"      more head mass, earlier knee: {frac(P2(8))} -> k* = {knee_at(P2, tau)}"
          f" ;  {frac(Q2(8))} -> k* = {knee_at(Q2, tau)}")
    print("      => the SIGN of a measured head-mass/knee correlation carries no")
    print("         information about the underlying mechanism.")

    print("\n  (c) Tail shape dominates the head: identical first eight keys,")
    print("      knees arbitrarily far apart:")
    for N in (10, 100, 1000):
        A = staged_profile(F(1, 2), tau, 8, 9)
        B = staged_profile(F(1, 2), tau, 8, 9 + N)
        same = all(A(j) == B(j) for j in range(9))
        print(f"      N = {N:>5}: heads identical through key 8? {same};"
              f"  k*(A) = {knee_at(A, tau)}, k*(B) = {knee_at(B, tau)}")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Quantitative tail shape
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------


def part_six_tail_shape() -> None:
    rule("6. Tail shape, quantitatively: geometric vs. Pareto residuals")
    r = 8

    print("  Geometric residual  1 - cum(r+j) <= R * rho^j:")
    print(f"  {'tau':>7} {'R':>5} {'rho':>5} {'least j with R rho^j <= 1-tau':>32} {'bound k* <=':>12}")
    R, rr = F(1, 2), F(1, 2)
    for tau in (F(9, 10), F(99, 100), F(999, 1000)):
        j = 0
        while R * rr ** j > F(1) - tau:
            j += 1
        print(f"  {float(tau):>7.3f} {frac(R):>5} {frac(rr):>5} {j:>32} {r + j:>12}")
    print("  -> a geometric tail gives a LOGARITHMIC knee: k* <= r + log(R/(1-tau))/log(1/rho).")

    print("\n  Pareto (heavy) residual  1 - cum(r+j) >= R/(j+1):")
    print(f"  {'tau':>7} {'R':>5} {'forced k* - r + 1 >= R/(1-tau)':>34}")
    R = F(1, 2)
    for tau in (F(9, 10), F(99, 100), F(999, 1000)):
        print(f"  {float(tau):>7.3f} {frac(R):>5} {float(R / (1 - tau)):>34.1f}")
    print("  -> a Pareto tail gives a LINEAR-in-1/(1-tau) knee, diverging as tau -> 1.")
    print("  The same head can sit above either tail: only the tail decides.")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 7. The participation ratio (l^2) bound
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------


def key_masses(cum: CaptureCurve, k: int) -> List[F]:
    return [cum(j + 1) - cum(j) for j in range(k)]


def collision_mass(cum: CaptureCurve, k: int) -> F:
    """Inverse participation ratio of the k heaviest keys: sum of squared masses."""
    return sum(m * m for m in key_masses(cum, k))


def part_seven_participation() -> None:
    rule("7. The participation bound  k* >= tau^2 / C")
    tau = F(9, 10)
    print(f"  tolerance tau = {frac(tau)}\n")
    print("  Cauchy-Schwarz on the capture curve:  cum(k)^2 <= k * C(k).")
    for k in (5, 10, 40):
        P = uniform_profile(tau, k)
        C = collision_mass(P, k)
        lhs = P(k) ** 2
        print(f"    uniform over {k:>2} keys: cum(k)^2 = {frac(lhs):>12},"
              f"  k*C(k) = {frac(F(k) * C):>12},  C(k) = {frac(C):>10} (= tau^2/k)")
    print("    -> equality for the uniform profile: the bound is attained.")

    print("\n  Consequence: if the collision mass never exceeds C then k* >= tau^2/C.")
    print(f"  {'C':>10} {'tau^2/C':>10} {'a witness profile':>26} {'its k*':>8}")
    for k in (5, 20, 100):
        P = uniform_profile(tau, k)
        C = max(collision_mass(P, n) for n in range(1, k + 2))
        print(f"  {float(C):>10.5f} {float(tau ** 2 / C):>10.3f}"
              f" {'uniform over ' + str(k) + ' keys':>26} {knee_at(P, tau):>8}")

    print("\n  One-sidedness: for any collision budget C > 0 and any target N there")
    print("  is a profile with collision mass <= C at every prefix and k* >= N.")
    C = F(1, 100)
    for N in (50, 500):
        k = max(N, int(tau / C) + 1)
        P = uniform_profile(tau, k)
        worst = max(collision_mass(P, n) for n in range(1, k + 2))
        print(f"    C = {frac(C)}, N = {N:>4}:  uniform over {k} keys has"
              f" max collision {float(worst):.6f} <= {float(C)} and k* = {knee_at(P, tau)}")
    print("\n  So the participation ratio pins the knee from below and not at all")
    print("  from above -- the generic shape of every scalar head statistic.")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# main
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------


def main() -> None:
    part_one_audit()
    part_two_robustness()
    part_three_power()
    part_four_tail_reduction()
    part_five_decoupling()
    part_six_tail_shape()
    part_seven_participation()
    rule("Summary")
    print("""  * The three reported coefficients (-0.60 / +0.80 / -0.40) are not what
    the tabulated numbers give: exactly, +7/(2*sqrt 95), -11/38, -8/sqrt 95.
  * At five domains a |rho| >= 0.7 bar has exact size 7/30 ~ 0.233.
  * The knee is a functional of the tail alone; head mass constrains it not
    at all, and the sign of any head/knee correlation is free.
  * Concentration statistics bound the knee from below only: k* >= tau^2/C,
    attained by the uniform profile, with no upper bound of any kind.""")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

demos.name: Decoupling Laboratory: One Head Mass, Every Possible Knee
demos.description: Builds staged capture curves — head mass h held through key r, then a linear ramp reaching the tolerance exactly at key k — and uses them to exhibit three impossibility results in exact arithmetic. First, a single top-8 mass of 1/2 realised with knees 9, 12, 25, 200 and 5000, proving no function can map head mass to the knee. Second, one domain pair in which more head mass accompanies a later knee and another in which it accompanies an earlier one, proving the sign of any measured head/knee correlation is mechanistically uninformative. Third, pairs of curves pointwise identical through key 8 — same top-8 mass, same head entropy, same value of every head statistic — whose knees differ by a prescribed amount N.

demos.name: Memory-Budget Calculator: What Tail Shape Costs as Coverage Tightens
demos.description: Sweeps the tolerance from 0.9 to 0.9999 and reports, for a fixed head budget, the key budget implied by a light geometric residual R*rho^j against the budget forced by a heavy Pareto residual R/(j+1). The geometric regime grows logarithmically in 1/(1-tau) while the Pareto regime grows linearly, so the two diverge by more than two orders of magnitude at four-nines coverage. Since identical heads can sit above either tail, this gap is invisible to every statistic of the peak — the practical content of the tail mechanism for anyone sizing an attention cache.
demos.code:
"""Memory-budget calculator: what tail shape costs you as coverage tightens.

For a fixed head budget r, compares the key budget implied by a light
(geometric) residual  R rho^j  against the budget forced by a heavy (Pareto)
residual  R/(j+1), across a sweep of tolerances tau.  The two regimes are
invisible to any statistic of the head, yet they differ by orders of magnitude
at high coverage -- the practical content of the tail mechanism.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction as F
from typing import List, Tuple


def geometric_budget(tau: F, R: F, rho: F, r: int, jmax: int = 100000) -> int:
    """Least r + j with R rho^j <= 1 - tau: an upper bound on the knee."""
    term = R
    for j in range(jmax + 1):
        if term <= 1 - tau:
            return r + j
        term *= rho
    raise ValueError("no j found")


def pareto_budget(tau: F, R: F, r: int) -> F:
    """Forced lower bound r + R/(1-tau) - 1 for a Pareto residual."""
    return r + R / (1 - tau) - 1


def sweep(taus: List[F], R: F, rho: F, r: int) -> List[Tuple[F, int, float]]:
    return [(tau, geometric_budget(tau, R, rho, r), float(pareto_budget(tau, R, r)))
            for tau in taus]


def main() -> None:
    R, rho, r = F(1, 2), F(1, 2), 8
    taus = [F(9, 10), F(95, 100), F(99, 100), F(999, 1000), F(9999, 10000)]
    print(f"head budget r = {r},  residual scale R = {R},  geometric ratio = {rho}\n")
    print(f"{'tau':>9} {'light-tail k* <=':>18} {'heavy-tail k* >=':>18} {'ratio':>9}")
    for tau, g, p in sweep(taus, R, rho, r):
        print(f"{float(tau):>9.4f} {g:>18} {p:>18.1f} {p / g:>9.2f}")
    print("\nA geometric tail costs O(log 1/(1-tau)) keys; a Pareto tail costs")
    print("Theta(1/(1-tau)) keys.  Identical heads can sit above either tail,")
    print("so no head statistic distinguishes these two engineering worlds.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

algorithms.name: Exact Midrank Spearman Correlation in Rational Arithmetic
algorithms.description: Computes Spearman's rank correlation without floating point. Each column is replaced by midranks — one plus the count of strictly smaller entries plus half the count of ties — which handles tied observations by the standard average-rank correction. The rank covariance S_xy and the two rank variances are then exact rationals. Because rho = S_xy/sqrt(S_xx S_yy), the coefficient is exactly rational whenever the two columns share a tie pattern (so S_xx = S_yy) and otherwise a rational multiple of an inverse square root; the routine detects the perfect-square case and returns the symbolic form in the other, so no rounding ever enters an audit. Complexity is O(n^2) per column by direct counting, reducible to O(n log n) by sorting; on the five-row table it is instantaneous. This is the routine that produces 7/(2*sqrt 95), -11/38 and -8/sqrt 95 in place of the reported -0.60, +0.80 and -0.40.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT : columns x, y of n exact rational values
OUTPUT: rank covariance S_xy and the exact value of Spearman's rho

1. function MIDRANKS(x):
2.     for i in 1..n:
3.         smaller <- |{ j : x[j] <  x[i] }|
4.         tied    <- |{ j : x[j] == x[i] }|
5.         r[i]    <- 1 + smaller + (tied - 1)/2        # exact rational
6.     return r
7.
8. function RANKCOV(x, y):
9.     rx <- MIDRANKS(x) ; ry <- MIDRANKS(y)
10.    mx <- (sum rx)/n  ; my <- (sum ry)/n             # both equal (n+1)/2
11.    return sum_i (rx[i] - mx) * (ry[i] - my)
12.
13. function SPEARMAN_EXACT(x, y):
14.    Sxy <- RANKCOV(x, y)
15.    Sxx <- RANKCOV(x, x) ; Syy <- RANKCOV(y, y)
16.    P   <- Sxx * Syy
17.    if numerator(P) and denominator(P) are perfect squares:
18.        return Sxy / sqrt(P)                          # exact rational
19.    else:
20.        return symbolic "Sxy / sqrt(P)"               # never round
algorithms.code:
"""Algorithm A: exact midrank Spearman correlation in rational arithmetic."""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction as F
from math import isqrt
from typing import List, Sequence, Tuple


def midranks(x: Sequence[F]) -> List[F]:
    """Average ('midrank') ranks of a column, ties sharing the average rank.

    r(i) = 1 + #{j : x_j < x_i} + (#{j : x_j = x_i} - 1)/2
    """
    out: List[F] = []
    for xi in x:
        smaller = sum(1 for xj in x if xj < xi)
        tied = sum(1 for xj in x if xj == xi)
        out.append(F(1) + smaller + F(tied - 1, 2))
    return out


def rank_covariance(x: Sequence[F], y: Sequence[F]) -> F:
    """S_xy = sum_i (r_x(i) - mean r_x)(r_y(i) - mean r_y), exactly."""
    rx, ry = midranks(x), midranks(y)
    mx = sum(rx) / len(rx)
    my = sum(ry) / len(ry)
    return sum((a - mx) * (b - my) for a, b in zip(rx, ry))


def spearman_exact(x: Sequence[F], y: Sequence[F]) -> Tuple[F, F, str]:
    """Return (S_xy, S_xx*S_yy, symbolic rho).

    rho = S_xy / sqrt(S_xx S_yy).  When S_xx = S_yy the value is rational and
    is returned as such; otherwise the exact symbolic form is returned so that
    no floating point ever enters the audit.
    """
    sxy = rank_covariance(x, y)
    sxx = rank_covariance(x, x)
    syy = rank_covariance(y, y)
    prod = sxx * syy
    # Is the product a perfect rational square?
    num, den = prod.numerator, prod.denominator
    rn, rd = isqrt(num), isqrt(den)
    if rn * rn == num and rd * rd == den:
        rho = sxy / F(rn, rd)
        return sxy, prod, f"{rho.numerator}/{rho.denominator}"
    return sxy, prod, f"({sxy}) / sqrt({prod})"


def audit_table() -> None:
    """Recompute the three reported coefficients of the five-domain table."""
    entropy = [F(3798, 1000), F(3801, 1000), F(3615, 1000), F(3752, 1000), F(3864, 1000)]
    top8 = [F(488, 1000), F(488, 1000), F(526, 1000), F(502, 1000), F(473, 1000)]
    head = [F(83, 1000), F(82, 1000), F(86, 1000), F(80, 1000), F(79, 1000)]
    kstar = [F(12), F(16), F(16), F(20), F(24)]

    for name, col, reported in (("entropy", entropy, -0.60),
                                ("top-8 mass", top8, +0.80),
                                ("head agreement", head, -0.40)):
        sxy, prod, rho = spearman_exact(col, kstar)
        print(f"{name:<16} S = {sxy}   rho = {rho}   (reported {reported:+.2f})")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    audit_table()

algorithms.name: Exact Permutation Null and Bar-Size Calculus for Rank Correlation
algorithms.description: Determines, exactly and without asymptotic approximation, how often a pre-registered threshold on |rho| fires by chance. The engine is the displacement identity rho = 1 - 6D/(n(n^2-1)), where D = sum (r_i-s_i)^2 is the squared rank distance; it follows from the fact that both rank vectors are permutations of {1,...,n}, so their sums and sums of squares are fixed. Consequently the null distribution of rho over pairs of rankings is the distribution of the displacement statistic of the single permutation relating them, and enumerating S_n gives the exact distribution as a finite lattice. From it one reads the exact two-sided size of any |rho| >= t bar, the exact one-sided p-value of any observed D, and the least sample size at which a given threshold attains a given level. Complexity O(n! * n), exact and feasible to about n = 11; at n = 5 it returns 7/30 for the 0.7 bar and the pair 7/60, 1/24 for the two admissible tie-breaks of the strongest column.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT : sample size n, threshold t in (0,1], observed displacement D_obs
OUTPUT: exact size of the '|rho| >= t' bar and the exact one-sided p-value

1. function DISPLACEMENT(sigma):
2.     return sum_i (sigma(i) - i)^2
3.
4. function NULL_DISTRIBUTION(n):
5.     dist <- empty multiset
6.     for each sigma in S_n:                            # n! permutations
7.         dist[ DISPLACEMENT(sigma) ] += 1
8.     return dist
9.
10. function RHO_OF_D(D, n):
11.    return 1 - 6D / (n(n^2 - 1))                      # exact rational
12.
13. function BAR_SIZE(n, t):
14.    dist <- NULL_DISTRIBUTION(n)
15.    hits <- sum of dist[D] over all D with |RHO_OF_D(D,n)| >= t
16.    return hits / n!                                  # exact fraction
17.
18. function ONE_SIDED_PVALUE(n, D_obs):
19.    dist <- NULL_DISTRIBUTION(n)
20.    return (sum of dist[D] for D >= D_obs) / n!
21.
22. function SMALLEST_N_FOR_LEVEL(t, level):
23.    for n = 3, 4, 5, ...:
24.        if BAR_SIZE(n, t) <= level: return n

algorithms.name: Knee Localisation with Tail Reduction and Participation Bounds
algorithms.description: The structural toolkit for a capture curve given as a monotone oracle. The knee — the least budget k with c(k) >= tau — is located by exponential search followed by bisection, costing O(log k*) oracle calls by monotonicity. The same routine applied to the shifted curve j -> c(r+j) computes the tail knee, and the pair verifies the exact reduction k* = r + tailKnee whenever the head budget r falls short of the tolerance; this identity is what makes the knee a functional of the residual alone. Key masses are obtained by differencing in O(k) and their squares summed to give the collision mass C(k), the inverse participation ratio, from which the attained lower bound k* >= tau^2/C follows by Cauchy-Schwarz. Two tail-shape estimators complete the kit: a geometric upper bound, returning the first index at which R*rho^j falls below the missing mass 1-tau, and a Pareto lower bound r + R/(1-tau) - 1 forced by a residual that stays above R/(j+1). Constructors for the uniform and staged reference families are included, so every bound can be exercised on curves whose knees are known in closed form.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT : capture-curve oracle c, tolerance tau, head budget r
OUTPUT: knee, tail knee, collision mass, and the two tail-shape bounds

1. function KNEE_AT(c, tau):                             # O(log k*) oracle calls
2.     if c(0) >= tau: return 0
3.     lo <- 0 ; hi <- 1
4.     while c(hi) < tau:  lo <- hi ; hi <- 2*hi          # exponential search
5.     while lo + 1 < hi:                                 # bisection
6.         mid <- (lo + hi) / 2
7.         if c(mid) >= tau: hi <- mid  else: lo <- mid
8.     return hi
9.
10. function TAIL_KNEE(c, r, tau):
11.    return KNEE_AT( j -> c(r + j), tau )
12.
13. function TAIL_REDUCTION_CHECK(c, r, tau):             # requires c(r) < tau
14.    return KNEE_AT(c, tau) == r + TAIL_KNEE(c, r, tau) # always true
15.
16. function COLLISION_MASS(c, k):
17.    return sum_{j < k} ( c(j+1) - c(j) )^2             # O(k)
18.
19. function PARTICIPATION_LOWER_BOUND(tau, C):
20.    return tau^2 / C                                   # attained by the uniform domain
21.
22. function GEOMETRIC_KNEE_BOUND(tau, R, rho, r):
23.    j <- 0 ; term <- R
24.    while term > 1 - tau:  j <- j + 1 ; term <- term * rho
25.    return r + j                                       # upper bound on k*
26.
27. function PARETO_KNEE_BOUND(tau, R, r):
28.    return r + R/(1 - tau) - 1                         # lower bound on k*

visualizations.name: One Head, Four Knees: Capture Curves and Their Residual Decay
visualizations.description: A two-panel figure making the tail mechanism visible. The upper panel draws four capture curves that are pointwise identical through key 8 — identical top-8 mass, identical head entropy, identical value of every statistic computable from the head — but whose knees at tolerance 0.9 are 9, 20, 40 and 80. The lower panel plots the corresponding residuals 1 - c(k) on a logarithmic axis against the missing-mass line 1 - tau, showing that the knee is precisely the first crossing and that the crossing point is a property of the decay rate, not of the peak.
visualizations.code:
"""Visualization: two domains, one head, two very different knees.

Draws capture curves for a family of staged profiles that are pointwise
identical through key 8 -- same top-8 mass, same head entropy, same value of
every statistic computable from the head -- but whose knees at tolerance
tau = 0.9 are 9, 20, 40 and 80.  Below it, the residual curves 1 - c(k) are
plotted on a logarithmic axis to show the light (geometric) versus heavy
(Pareto) decay regimes that actually decide the knee.

Requires matplotlib; writes knee_tail_mechanism.png.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Callable, List

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

TAU: float = 0.9
HEAD_MASS: float = 0.5
HEAD_BUDGET: int = 8


def staged_curve(h: float, tau: float, r: int, k: int) -> Callable[[int], float]:
    step = (tau - h) / (k - r)
    return lambda j: 0.0 if j == 0 else min(1.0, h + max(j - r, 0) * step)


def knee(curve: Callable[[int], float], tau: float, cap: int = 5000) -> int:
    for k in range(cap):
        if curve(k) >= tau:
            return k
    return cap


def main() -> None:
    knees: List[int] = [9, 20, 40, 80]
    xs = np.arange(0, 100)

    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(9, 8.5), sharex=True)

    for k in knees:
        c = staged_curve(HEAD_MASS, TAU, HEAD_BUDGET, k)
        ys = [c(int(x)) for x in xs]
        ax1.step(xs, ys, where="post", lw=1.8, label=f"knee $k^*={knee(c, TAU)}$")
        ax2.semilogy(xs, [max(1e-6, 1.0 - c(int(x))) for x in xs], lw=1.8)

    ax1.axhline(TAU, color="k", ls="--", lw=1, label=r"tolerance $\tau=0.9$")
    ax1.axvline(HEAD_BUDGET, color="grey", ls=":", lw=1)
    ax1.annotate("identical through key 8\n(same top-8 mass, same head entropy)",
                 xy=(HEAD_BUDGET, HEAD_MASS), xytext=(20, 0.28),
                 arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="grey"), fontsize=9,
                 color="dimgrey")
    ax1.set_ylabel("capture curve $c(k)$")
    ax1.set_title("One head, four knees: the tail decides", fontsize=13)
    ax1.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=9)
    ax1.set_ylim(0, 1.02)
    ax1.grid(alpha=0.3)

    ax2.axhline(1 - TAU, color="k", ls="--", lw=1)
    ax2.text(62, (1 - TAU) * 1.25, r"missing mass $1-\tau$", fontsize=9)
    ax2.set_xlabel("key budget $k$")
    ax2.set_ylabel(r"residual $1-c(k)$  (log scale)")
    ax2.set_title("The knee is where the residual first dips below $1-\\tau$",
                  fontsize=12)
    ax2.grid(alpha=0.3, which="both")

    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("knee_tail_mechanism.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote knee_tail_mechanism.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

visualizations.name: The Exact Null Lattice of Spearman's Coefficient at Five Domains
visualizations.description: Enumerates all 120 permutations of five items, converts each squared rank displacement to rho = 1 - D/20, and plots the resulting lattice distribution with the |rho| >= 0.7 rejection region shaded. Only twenty-one values of rho exist at this sample size, and 28 of the 120 orderings land in the rejection region — the exact 7/30 false-positive rate. The three recomputed coefficients of the five-domain table are overlaid, showing at a glance that only head agreement reaches the bar and how far the reported values sit from the truth.
visualizations.code:
"""Visualization: the exact null distribution of Spearman's rho at n = 5.

Enumerates all 120 permutations of five items, tabulates the squared rank
displacement D, converts to rho = 1 - D/20, and plots the resulting lattice
distribution with the |rho| >= 0.7 rejection region shaded.  The three
recomputed coefficients of the five-domain table are marked, together with the
two admissible readings of the tied knee column, showing how the pre-registered
bar and the tie interact.

Requires matplotlib; writes spearman_null_n5.png.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from collections import Counter
from itertools import permutations
from typing import Dict

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def displacement(p) -> int:
    return sum((p[i] - i) ** 2 for i in range(len(p)))


def main() -> None:
    dist: Dict[int, int] = Counter(displacement(p) for p in permutations(range(5)))
    rhos = sorted((1 - D / 20, c) for D, c in dist.items())
    xs = [r for r, _ in rhos]
    ys = [c for _, c in rhos]
    colors = ["#c0392b" if abs(r) >= 0.7 - 1e-9 else "#95a5a6" for r in xs]

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 5.2))
    ax.bar(xs, ys, width=0.07, color=colors, edgecolor="white")

    bar_mass = sum(c for r, c in rhos if abs(r) >= 0.7 - 1e-9)
    ax.set_title(
        f"Exact null distribution of Spearman's $\\rho$ at $n=5$ "
        f"(shaded: $|\\rho|\\geq0.7$, {bar_mass}/120 = 7/30 $\\approx$ 23.3%)",
        fontsize=12)
    ax.set_xlabel(r"$\rho = 1 - D/20$")
    ax.set_ylabel("number of permutations")
    ax.grid(alpha=0.25, axis="y")

    marks = [(-0.8208, "head agreement  $-8/\\sqrt{95}$", "#1f77b4"),
             (+0.3591, "entropy  $7/(2\\sqrt{95})$", "#2ca02c"),
             (-0.2895, "top-8 mass  $-11/38$", "#e67e22")]
    for x, label, col in marks:
        ax.axvline(x, color=col, lw=2)
        ax.annotate(label, xy=(x, max(ys) * 0.92), xytext=(x, max(ys) * 1.03),
                    fontsize=8.5, color=col, ha="center")

    ax.set_ylim(0, max(ys) * 1.22)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("spearman_null_n5.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote spearman_null_n5.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

interactive_demos.title: The Knee Laboratory: Drag the Head, Drag the Tail, Watch Which One Matters
interactive_demos.description: A live capture-curve sandbox. Three sliders control the mass sitting on the first eight keys, the exponent alpha governing how the residual decays like j^-alpha, and the tolerance tau. The canvas draws the capture curve as a step function with the tolerance line, marks the knee, and — in green — draws the participation lower bound tau^2/C computed live from the collision mass of the retained keys. Preset buttons contrast a light tail against a heavy one at equal head mass, and a large head against a small one at equal tail. The readout panel reports top-8 mass, residual, collision mass and the bound, and confirms that the bound never crosses the knee. Two progressively disclosed sections explain the exact tail-reduction identity and the Cauchy-Schwarz derivation of the bound, including why it is attained and why it can have no upper-bound companion. The intended discovery is visceral: the head slider moves the knee barely and in either direction, the tail slider moves it by an order of magnitude.
interactive_demos.html:
The Knee Laboratory

A capture curve $c(k)$ records how much attention mass the $k$ heaviest keys carry. The knee $k^\ast$ is the smallest budget with $c(k)\ge\tau$. Move the sliders: the head controls how much mass sits on the first eight keys, the tail exponent controls how the remaining mass decays. Watch what actually moves the knee — and what does not.
capture curve $c(k)$   tolerance $\tau$   knee $k^\ast$   participation lower bound $\tau^2/C$
measured
top-8 mass  0.500
knee  —
residual after 8 keys  —
collision mass $C(k^\ast)$  —
participation bound $\tau^2/C$  —
Why does the head barely matter?

Because of an exact identity. If the first $r$ keys fall short of the tolerance, $c(r)<\tau$, then $$k^\ast(\tau) \;=\; r \;+\; \min\{\,j : c(r+j)\ge\tau\,\}.$$ The second term is computed entirely inside the residual curve. Two domains whose capture curves agree from key $r$ onwards therefore have exactly the same knee, however different their heads are. Try the two "heavy tail" presets: the head mass changes by a factor of four and the knee hardly notices.

What is the green bound?

Write $m_j=c(j+1)-c(j)$ for the mass on the $j$-th key and $C(k)=\sum_{j<k} m_j^2$ for the collision mass (the reciprocal of the effective number of participating keys). Cauchy–Schwarz on $c(k)=\sum_{j<k}m_j$ gives $c(k)^2\le k\,C(k)$, and at the knee $c(k^\ast)\ge\tau$, so $$k^\ast \;\ge\; \frac{\tau^2}{C(k^\ast)}.$$ The bound is attained: a domain spreading mass evenly over $k$ keys has collision mass exactly $\tau^2/k$ at its knee $k$. But it is one-sided — no concentration statistic gives an upper bound, because mass can always be pushed further into the tail without changing any concentration budget.

interactive_demos.title: Rank-Correlation Roulette: Exact Coefficients, Exact Thresholds, and the Tie That Decides
interactive_demos.description: A two-part statistical instrument. The upper panel displays the five-domain table and recomputes all three rank correlations live from midranks, printing the exact symbolic value beside the reported one so the inverted ranking is immediate; two buttons toggle the admissible readings of the tied knee column and show the strongest effect flipping between an exact one-sided p-value of 7/60 (not significant) and 1/24 (significant). The lower panel enumerates the full permutation null for a chosen sample size between four and eight items, draws the lattice distribution of rho with the rejection region shaded, and reports the exact size of the |rho| >= t bar as a reduced fraction together with the probability that at least one of three independent predictors clears it by luck. Sliding n from 5 upward shows the 0.7 bar falling from 23% toward a defensible level, and collapsible sections derive the rho = 1 - 6D/(n(n^2-1)) identity and spell out the design implication.
interactive_demos.html:
Rank-Correlation Roulette

Two questions about a five-row table. First: what are the rank correlations, computed exactly? Second: how often would a threshold like $|\rho|\ge 0.7$ fire on pure noise at this sample size? Both answers are exact fractions, and you can watch them move.

1  The five-domain table, recomputed

tie in the knee column: prose-en = math = 16
How the coefficients are computed

Each column is replaced by its midranks: one plus the number of strictly smaller entries, plus half the number of ties. With $\bar r=3$ for five items, $S_{xy}=\sum_i (r_x(i)-3)(r_y(i)-3)$ and $\rho = S_{xy}/\sqrt{S_{xx}S_{yy}}$. The knee column has one tie, so $S_{kk}=19/2$ rather than $10$.

The three exact values are $7/(2\sqrt{95})$, $-11/38$ and $-8/\sqrt{95}$. Note the last column: French prose has the smallest top-8 mass and the largest knee, which by itself drags the top-8 correlation negative.

2  What the threshold actually costs you


5

0.70
Why $\rho$ lives on a lattice

For two full rankings of $n$ items, let $D=\sum_i (r_i-s_i)^2$. Because both rank vectors are permutations of $\{1,\dots,n\}$, their sums and sums of squares are fixed, and expanding gives the classical identity $$\rho = 1 - \frac{6D}{n(n^2-1)}.$$ At $n=5$ this is $\rho = 1 - D/20$, and $D$ is an even integer in $[0,40]$: only twenty-one values of $\rho$ are achievable at all. Enumerating the $120$ permutations shows exactly $28$ of them reach $|\rho|\ge0.7$, so the bar has exact size $28/120 = 7/30 \approx 0.233$.

The design implication

Fire a $23\%$ test at three independent predictors and the chance that at least one "confirms" by luck is $1-(23/30)^3\approx 0.55$. A verdict of "one confirmed, one partial, one refuted" out of three is the modal outcome of pure noise at five domains. Push the $n$ slider: the $0.7$ bar only becomes a genuine $5\%$ test at nine domains. More layers or more sampling windows do not help — $n$ counts domains.

interactive_layout:
# Where the Knee Lives ### A guided tour of attention budgets, exact rank statistics, and why the tail wins --- ## 0 · The question in one picture Sort every key an attention mechanism can look at, heaviest first, and start filling a bag. The **capture curve** $c(k)$ tells you how much of the total attention mass the first $k$ keys carry. Fix a tolerance $\tau$ — say $0.9$ — and the **knee** is the smallest budget that gets you there: $$k^\ast(\tau) \;=\; \min\{\,k : c(k) \ge \tau\,\}.$$ That single integer is the memory budget. Everything below is about what determines it. The natural guess is *concentration*: a distribution with a tall peak should need fewer keys. Play with the laboratory below before reading on. Move the **head mass** slider — how much sits on the first eight keys — and then move the **tail exponent** slider. One of them moves the knee. It is not the one you expect. {{interactive_demo:0}}
What you should have noticed — click after playing Dragging the head mass from $0.2$ to $0.8$ barely shifts the knee, and can shift it in *either* direction. Dragging the tail exponent from $0.6$ to $3.5$ moves it by an order of magnitude. That asymmetry is not an artefact of this particular curve family — it is a theorem, and §2 proves it. The green dashed line is a genuine lower bound coming from the $\ell^2$ concentration of the retained keys. Notice that it *never* crosses to the right of the knee, and notice how far to the left it can sit. That gap is exactly the room the tail has to work in.
--- ## 1 · The empirical claim, and the arithmetic A structural study measured three scalar descriptors across five text domains and correlated each against the knee at context length $512$: | domain | entropy | top-8 mass | head agreement | knee | |---|---|---|---|---| | code | 3.798 | 0.488 | 0.083 | 12 | | prose-en | 3.801 | 0.488 | 0.082 | 16 | | math | 3.615 | 0.526 | 0.086 | 16 | | prose-de | 3.752 | 0.502 | 0.080 | 20 | | prose-fr | 3.864 | 0.473 | 0.079 | >24 | The announced verdict: top-8 mass is the strongest predictor at $\rho = +0.80$, entropy a partial second at $-0.60$, cross-head agreement a dud at $-0.40$. Five rows. Three coefficients. Let us just compute them. {{algorithm:0}} Running that on the table gives $\rho(\text{entropy}) = 7/(2\sqrt{95}) \approx +0.359$, $\rho(\text{top-8}) = -11/38 \approx -0.289$, and $\rho(\text{head agreement}) = -8/\sqrt{95} \approx -0.821$. Every reported number is wrong in sign, in magnitude, or in both, and the ranking of the three predictors is *exactly reversed*: the column dismissed as "constant, not a differentiator" is the only one clearing the study's own $|\rho| \ge 0.7$ bar.
Where does the negative sign come from? Look at French prose: it has the *smallest* top-8 mass in the table ($0.473$) and the *largest* knee ($>24$). That single pairing — bottom rank on the predictor, top rank on the response — contributes $(1-3)(5-3) = -4$ to a rank covariance whose total is only $-11/4$. It dominates. Meanwhile code and English prose are tied at the bottom of the top-8 column and hold the two smallest knees, which pushes in the same negative direction. Two objections, both answerable. *Censoring:* French prose's knee is only known to be $>24$, but Spearman sees only ranks, and every value above $20$ leaves it in last place — so all readings give identical coefficients. *Tie-breaking:* there are two ties in the table, hence a handful of strict orderings; enumerate them all and top-8 stays negative in every single case, entropy stays positive, and head agreement stays at $-0.7$ or below.
--- ## 2 · What a threshold is worth at five data points Suppose the arithmetic had come out as reported. Would $\rho = +0.80$ on five domains have meant anything? At $n$ items, Spearman's coefficient is rigidly tied to the squared rank displacement $D = \sum_i (r_i - s_i)^2$: $$\rho \;=\; 1 - \frac{6D}{n(n^2-1)},$$ which at $n = 5$ reads $\rho = 1 - D/20$. Since $D$ is an even integer in $[0,40]$, only twenty-one values of $\rho$ exist at all. So we can *enumerate the entire null distribution* and read off the exact false-positive rate of any threshold — no asymptotics, no tables. {{algorithm:1}} The widget below does this live. Set $n = 5$ and $t = 0.7$ and read the fraction. {{interactive_demo:1}} The answer is $28/120 = 7/30 \approx 0.233$. **A $|\rho| \ge 0.7$ bar at five domains is a $23\%$ test.** Fire it at three predictors, as the study did, and the probability that at least one "confirms" by pure luck is about $55\%$ — so "one confirmed, one partial, one refuted" is the *modal* outcome of noise. The widget's tie-break buttons make the second point. The strongest column in the table, head agreement, has one-sided $p$-value $7/60 \approx 0.117$ under one admissible reading of the knee tie and $1/24 \approx 0.042$ under the other. A coin-flip about a tie decides whether the only real effect in the round is significant. Here is the whole null distribution drawn out, with the rejection region shaded and the three recomputed coefficients marked: {{visualization:1}}
How many domains would you need? Enumerating the null at each $n$ gives the exact size of the $|\rho| \ge 0.7$ bar: $$\frac{7}{30},\quad \frac{49}{360},\quad \frac{37}{420},\quad \frac{129}{2240},\quad \frac{109}{2520} \qquad\text{at } n = 5,6,7,8,9.$$ So the conventional $0.7$ threshold first becomes a genuine $5\%$ test at **nine domains**. And note what does *not* help: sampling more layers, more windows, or more context lengths within the same five domains. The permutation null is over orderings of domains; $n$ counts domains. The general lesson: because achievable $\rho$ values form a finite lattice at every $n$, a pre-registration can *choose* a threshold with a stated size instead of inheriting $0.7$ by convention.
--- ## 3 · The mechanism is a theorem Alongside the correlations the study offered a mechanism: *the knee is set by the residual spread after the top keys are captured, not by how concentrated the peak is.* That sentence is provable — and the proof is three lines. > **Tail Reduction.** If the $r$ heaviest keys fall short of the tolerance, $c(r) < \tau$, then > $$k^\ast(\tau) \;=\; r \;+\; \min\{\,j : c(r+j) \ge \tau\,\}.$$
Proof Since $c(r) < \tau$ and $c$ is non-decreasing, no budget below $r$ reaches the tolerance, so $k^\ast \ge r$; write $k^\ast = r + j_0$. Then $c(r + j_0) \ge \tau$, so the minimum $j$ is at most $j_0$. Conversely, the budget $r + \min\{j : c(r+j) \ge \tau\}$ meets the tolerance, so $k^\ast$ is at most that. The two inequalities give equality. $\blacksquare$
The immediate corollary is the mechanism sentence itself: > **The knee is a functional of the tail.** If two capture curves agree from index $r$ onward, and neither reaches the tolerance by $r$, they have exactly the same knee — however differently their heads behave. Now, how completely does the head fail to constrain the knee? Completely. Consider **staged profiles**: put mass $h$ on the first key, hold flat through key $r$, then ramp linearly to hit $\tau$ exactly at key $k$. Head mass and knee become independent dials. {{demo:1}} Three consequences, each dismantling a piece of the original argument: 1. **No law exists.** The same top-8 mass $1/2$ is compatible with a knee of $9$, of $25$, of $5000$. So *no function whatsoever* maps top-8 mass to the knee — not linear, not monotone, not wild. 2. **The sign is free.** There are domain pairs where more head mass goes with a later knee, and pairs where it goes with an earlier one. A positive measured correlation is therefore not evidence for the tail mechanism — and neither is a negative one. Whatever the data had shown, it would have been compatible. *A test that cannot fail is not a test.* 3. **The tail can be arbitrarily loud.** For every $N$ there are two domains identical on their first eight keys — same top-8 mass, same head entropy, same *any* head statistic — whose knees differ by at least $N$. {{visualization:0}} --- ## 4 · What the tail actually does Having established that the tail decides, we can be quantitative. Two regimes bracket everything: **Light (geometric) tail.** If the residual $1 - c(r+j)$ decays like $R\rho^{\,j}$, the knee arrives as soon as $R\rho^{\,j}$ dips below the missing mass $1-\tau$: $$k^\ast \;\le\; r + \frac{\log\big(R/(1-\tau)\big)}{\log(1/\rho)} \qquad \text{— logarithmic.}$$ **Heavy (Pareto) tail.** If the residual stays above $R/(j+1)$, then $$k^\ast \;\ge\; r + \frac{R}{1-\tau} - 1 \qquad \text{— linear in } \tfrac{1}{1-\tau}\text{, diverging as } \tau \to 1.$$ The engineering gap between these is enormous, and — by the previous section — completely invisible to any head statistic. Here it is in numbers: {{demo:2}} At $\tau = 0.9$ the two regimes differ by a factor of about one; at $\tau = 0.9999$ they differ by a factor of over two hundred. If you are sizing a memory budget, *fit the decay*, don't measure the peak. {{algorithm:2}} --- ## 5 · Why every peak statistic fails the same way There is a satisfying structural reason for all of this, and it comes from the $\ell^2$ language physicists use for localisation. Write $m_j = c(j+1) - c(j)$ for the mass on the $j$-th heaviest key, and define the **collision mass** (inverse participation ratio) of the top $k$ keys: $$C(k) \;=\; \sum_{j The bound is exactly attained — and exactly one-sided **Attainment.** The uniform domain splitting mass $\tau/k$ over $k$ keys has collision mass $k \cdot (\tau/k)^2 = \tau^2/k$ at its own knee $k$, so $k^\ast \cdot C(k^\ast) = \tau^2$ precisely: Cauchy–Schwarz becomes an equality. The bound is not slack. **Refinement.** If every key mass is at most $m$, then $C(k) = \sum_{j 0$ and every target $N$ there is a domain with collision mass below $C$ at every prefix and knee at least $N$: take the uniform domain over $k \ge \max(N, \tau/C)$ keys, whose collision mass shrinks like $1/k$ while its knee grows like $k$. So there is provably **no** companion upper bound. This is the general shape. A concentration statistic of the head is a *lower-bound instrument*: it can certify the knee is not too early, never that it is not too late — because mass can always be pushed further out without changing any concentration budget. The half-line $[\tau^2/C, \infty)$ that the bound leaves open is precisely where tail shape does the deciding. Return to the laboratory in §0 with this in mind: the green line is the best any peak statistic can ever do, and the red line is free to run away from it. --- ## 6 · The whole thing, end to end {{demo:0}} --- ## 7 · Where this goes next - **A tail-exponent law.** The geometric and Pareto bounds are the endpoints of one family: for a residual decaying like $R j^{-\alpha}$ the knee should scale as $(R/(1-\tau))^{1/\alpha}$, interpolating logarithmic ($\alpha = \infty$) and linear ($\alpha = 1$) behaviour. That would turn tail-shape analysis from a diagnostic into a law with a measurable exponent per domain. - **A power calculus for small-$n$ claims.** The size $7/30$ is not special to five items; a closed form for $\text{size}(n,t)$ plus monotonicity in $n$ would let every study *choose* a bar with a stated size. - **Multi-statistic bounds.** Every individual concentration statistic is one-sided. Is a finite *family* ever two-sided under some tail-regularity hypothesis, such as log-convexity of the residual? - **Censored responses done properly.** Report the *set* of coefficients consistent with all admissible readings of a censored value, rather than imputing one. --- ## Further reading - [Spearman's rank correlation coefficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spearman%27s_rank_correlation_coefficient) — the $1 - 6D/(n(n^2-1))$ identity and its tie corrections. - [Permutation tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permutation_test) — exact inference by enumeration, which is what makes the $7/30$ figure a fact rather than an approximation. - [Inverse participation ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Participation_ratio) — the $\ell^2$ localisation measure borrowed here from condensed-matter physics. - [Heavy-tailed distributions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy-tailed_distribution) — why the difference between $\rho^{\,j}$ and $j^{-\alpha}$ decay is the difference between a small budget and an unbounded one. - [Cauchy–Schwarz inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%E2%80%93Schwarz_inequality) — one line of which yields the entire participation bound. **The moral.** The correlation was noise, the intuition behind it was a theorem, and the answer was never in the pile at the top. It was in the long thin tail of everything you almost left behind.
